title: Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46–52)
hookLine: a blind beggar shouts louder when told to hush, and Jesus asks: what do you want?
last: NOT TO BE SERVED, BUT TO SERVE.

lines: TOLD TO HUSH, HE SHOUTS LOUDER.
cards: Jericho, the last town before the long climb up to Jerusalem. Pilgrims are streaming through for the Passover, and Jesus is leaving town with a big crowd. By the side of the road sits a blind beggar.
Mark even gives his name: Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus. He hears it's Jesus of Nazareth passing, and he starts shouting. In the King James Bible: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me."
Shh. Not now. Don't embarrass us.
You know that feeling: your need is too loud, too much, badly timed. And Mark says he cried the more a great deal. He shouts louder.

teach.b: And Jesus stops. The whole crowd, going up to Jerusalem, stops because one blind man wouldn't be quiet. Call him, Jesus says.
And the same people who were shushing him turn around: "Be of good comfort, rise; he calleth thee."
Bartimaeus throws off his cloak, jumps up and comes. For a beggar, that cloak may have been his blanket and the cloth he caught coins on. He leaves it on the road.
Then Jesus asks a question that sounds almost too obvious: "What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?"

teach.h: THE SAME QUESTION AS JAMES AND JOHN.
teach.b: A few verses ago he asked James and John the very same thing, and they asked for the best seats in glory. This man asks for one thing, plainly: "Lord, that I might receive my sight." In Mark's Greek, the word isn't Lord.
It's Rabbouni, my teacher, a warm, personal word. Jesus says: go your way, your faith has made you whole.

teach.h: NAMED, AND FOLLOWING ON THE ROAD.
teach.b: Immediately he sees, and he follows Jesus on the road. Three things stand out.

teach.h: WHAT WILT THOU THAT I SHOULD DO UNTO THEE?
teach.b: He's the only person Mark ever names in a healing. He's the first in Mark to call Jesus son of David, the title of Israel's king, just as they reach Jerusalem.
And he's blind, yet he sees who Jesus is more clearly than the friends who asked for thrones.
Two blind men frame this whole stretch of the road: one who saw men like trees, slowly, and this one, who sees at once and follows.

how: Bartimaeus's cry, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me," is close to the Jesus Prayer that Orthodox and many other Christians repeat, and many Christians bring their plain requests to God in prayer as he did.

o: a tax collector who climbed a tree
a soldier who guarded the tomb
a blind beggar who asked Jesus for sight

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Bartimaeus is the only person Mark names in a healing
every other healed person in Mark goes unnamed.
when told to hush, he went quiet
he cried the more a great deal.
James and John were asked the same question
what do you want me to do for you? they asked for seats; he asked to see.

games.q: you're Bartimaeus, blind, by the road. Jesus is passing and the crowd tells you to be quiet. what do you do?
o: go quiet and wait for another day.
ask someone to lead you to him quietly.
games.why: "he cried the more a great deal." and Jesus stops the whole crowd to call him.

practice: Imagine someone who loves you stopping everything and asking, what do you want?
Not what you think you should want, not a list: one thing, plainly, the way Bartimaeus said it, maybe healing, courage, a job, or for someone to come home.
If you pray, say it to God just as plainly; if you don't, say it quietly to yourself, and notice how it feels to name it.

wordCard.voice: Bartimaeus. Son of Timaeus, a blind beggar at Jericho who wouldn't be hushed, who asked for his sight, and who followed on the road.

orig.note: Aramaic in Greek letters: my teacher, my master. what Bartimaeus calls Jesus in Mark 10:51.

carryVoice: Your line: what do you want? He named it, and followed. Jerusalem tomorrow.
